notes.front: In a twin, what is the critical engine?
notes.back: The engine whose failure has the most adverse effect on directional control.
notes.explanation: The published minimum control speed is determined with this engine inoperative.
notes.example: Like losing the one leg of a table that makes it tip worst, but in yaw rather than tilt.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 13 “Transition to Multiengine Airplanes”, “Derivation of VMC”, PDF p. 23
notes.evidence: The AFM/POH-published VMC is determined with the critical engine inoperative. The critical engine is the engine whose failure had the most adverse effect on directional control.

notes.front: What is the minimum control speed with the critical engine inoperative (VMC)?
notes.back: The calibrated airspeed at which, after a sudden critical loss of thrust, control of the aeroplane can be maintained.
notes.explanation: It is typically marked with a red radial line on most airspeed indicators.
introduces: minimum control speed with the critical engine inoperative
notes.example: Like the slowest speed at which a boat with one of two outboards dead can still be steered straight, but in the air.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 13 “Transition to Multiengine Airplanes”, “Terms and Definitions”, PDF p. 2
notes.evidence: VMC—currently defined in 14 CFR part 23, section 23.2135(c) as the calibrated airspeed at which, following the sudden critical loss of thrust, it is possible to maintain control of the airplane. VMC is typically marked with a red radial line on most airspeed indicators

notes.front: What is the best single-engine rate of climb speed (VYSE)?
notes.back: The best rate of climb speed with one engine inoperative, marked with a blue radial line on most airspeed indicators.
notes.explanation: Above the single-engine absolute ceiling, it gives the minimum rate of sink instead.
introduces: best single-engine rate of climb speed
notes.example: Like a cyclist's best climbing pace, but worked out for riding with one leg.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 13 “Transition to Multiengine Airplanes”, “Terms and Definitions”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: VYSE—best rate of climb speed with OEI. Marked with a blue radial line on most airspeed indicators. Above the single-engine absolute ceiling, VYSE yields the minimum rate of sink.

notes.front: What is the safe single-engine speed (VSSE)?
notes.back: The minimum speed at which the critical engine may be made inoperative intentionally.
notes.explanation: Its current name is safe, intentional one-engine-inoperative speed.
notes.example: Like the minimum speed an instructor sets before cutting a car's power steering in a skid lesson, but for shutting down an engine in flight.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 13 “Transition to Multiengine Airplanes”, “Terms and Definitions”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: VSSE—safe, intentional OEI speed—originally known as safe single-engine speed. It is the minimum speed to intentionally render the critical engine inoperative.

notes.front: What is propeller feathering?
notes.back: Setting an inoperative engine's propeller blades streamlined with the relative wind, which stops the engine turning and minimises propeller drag.
notes.explanation: Depending on single-engine performance, it often allows continued flight to a suitable airport after an engine failure.
notes.example: Like turning a canoe paddle edge-on to the water between strokes, but locked there for the rest of the flight.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 13 “Transition to Multiengine Airplanes”, “Feathering Propellers”, PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: The pilot of a typical multiengine airplane can feather the propeller of an inoperative engine. Since it stops engine rotation with the propeller blade streamlined with the airplane's relative wind, feathering the propeller of an inoperative engine minimizes propeller drag. [Figure 13-2] Depending upon single-engine performance, this feature often permits continued flight to a suitable airport following an engine failure.

notes.front: In a light twin, losing one engine loses half the power. By how much does climb performance fall?
notes.back: By 80 to 90 percent.
notes.explanation: In some cases a light twin may not be able to climb, or even hold altitude, after an engine failure.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 13 “Transition to Multiengine Airplanes”, “General”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: In a multiengine airplane, loss of thrust from one engine affects both performance and control. The most obvious problem is the loss of 50 percent of power, which reduces climb performance 80 to 90 percent. In some cases after an engine failure, the ability to climb or maintain altitude in a light-twin may not exist.

notes.front: Must a twin be able to climb at VMC?
notes.back: No; VMC addresses only directional control.
notes.explanation: Neither the current nor the older certification definition requires the aeroplane to climb at that speed.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 13 “Transition to Multiengine Airplanes”, “Terms and Definitions”, PDF p. 2
notes.evidence: There is no requirement under either determination that the airplane be capable of climbing at this airspeed. VMC only addresses directional control.
uses: minimum control speed with the critical engine inoperative

notes.front: On a twin whose engines both turn clockwise (seen from the pilot's seat), which engine is critical, and why?
notes.back: The left: the right engine's descending blade has the longer moment arm, so losing the left leaves the most asymmetrical thrust.
notes.explanation: With the left engine out, the right engine alone provides the remaining thrust, from further out.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 13 “Transition to Multiengine Airplanes”, “Derivation of VMC”, PDF p. 23
notes.evidence: and therefore has a longer moment arm than the descending propeller blade of the left engine. As a result, failure of the left engine will result in the most asymmetrical thrust (adverse yaw) as the right engine will be providing the remaining thrust.

notes.front: How does power on the operating engine affect VMC?
notes.back: VMC increases as power increases; with normally aspirated engines it is highest at takeoff power at sea level.
notes.explanation: It then decreases with altitude for normally aspirated engines.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 13 “Transition to Multiengine Airplanes”, “Derivation of VMC”, PDF p. 24
notes.evidence: VMC increases as power is increased on the operating engine. With normally aspirated engines, VMC is highest at takeoff power and sea level, and decreases with altitude.
uses: minimum control speed with the critical engine inoperative

notes.front: How does moving the centre of gravity aft affect VMC?
notes.back: VMC increases.
notes.explanation: An aft centre of gravity shortens the rudder's moment arm, reducing its effectiveness.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 13 “Transition to Multiengine Airplanes”, “Derivation of VMC”, PDF p. 24
notes.evidence: VMC increases as the center-of-gravity (CG) is moved aft. The moment arm of the rudder is reduced, and therefore its effectivity is reduced, as the CG is moved aft.
uses: minimum control speed with the critical engine inoperative

notes.front: In what state of the inoperative engine's propeller is VMC highest?
notes.back: Windmilling at the low pitch, high rpm blade angle.
notes.explanation: More drag on the inoperative engine means a higher VMC.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 13 “Transition to Multiengine Airplanes”, “Derivation of VMC”, PDF p. 24
notes.evidence: VMC increases with increased drag on the inoperative engine. VMC is highest, therefore, when the critical engine propeller is windmilling at the low pitch, high rpm blade angle.
uses: minimum control speed with the critical engine inoperative

notes.front: How does retracting the landing gear affect VMC?
notes.back: VMC increases.
notes.explanation: Extended landing gear aids directional stability, which tends to decrease VMC.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 13 “Transition to Multiengine Airplanes”, “Derivation of VMC”, PDF p. 25
notes.evidence: VMC increases when the landing gear is retracted. Extended landing gear aids directional stability, which tends to decrease VMC.
uses: minimum control speed with the critical engine inoperative

notes.front: How does reducing bank from 5° toward wings level affect VMC?
notes.back: VMC increases, possibly by more than 3 knots per degree.
notes.explanation: Since VMC is determined with up to 5° of bank, control may be lost almost 20 knots above published VMC with wings level.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 13 “Transition to Multiengine Airplanes”, “Derivation of VMC”, PDF p. 25
notes.evidence: VMC increases as bank angle decreases. In fact, VMC may increase more than 3 knots for each degree of bank reduction between 5° and wings-level. Since VMC was determined with up to 5° of bank, loss of directional control may be experienced at speeds almost 20 knots above published VMC when the wings are held level.
uses: minimum control speed with the critical engine inoperative

notes.front: In the 'identify' step after an engine failure, what should you mainly use to identify the failed engine?
notes.back: The control inputs needed to keep straight flight, not the engine gauges.
notes.explanation: Depending on the failure mode, the engine gauges may or may not confirm it.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 13 “Transition to Multiengine Airplanes”, “Configuration”, PDF p. 32
notes.evidence: The “identify” step is for the pilot to initially identify the failed engine. Confirmation on the engine gauges may or may not be possible, depending upon the failure mode. Identification should be primarily through the control inputs required to maintain straight flight, not the engine gauges.

notes.front: In the 'verify' step, how do you confirm which engine has failed?
notes.back: Retard the throttle of the suspected engine: no change in performance confirms it.
notes.explanation: The matching propeller control then goes fully aft to feather that engine.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 13 “Transition to Multiengine Airplanes”, “Configuration”, PDF p. 32
notes.evidence: The “verify” step directs the pilot to retard the throttle of the engine thought to have failed. No change in performance when the suspected throttle is retarded is verification that the correct engine has been identified as failed. The corresponding propeller control should be brought fully aft to feather the engine.

notes.front: When practising engine failures, what is the lowest speed at which one should ever be introduced?
notes.back: VSSE, or VYSE if no VSSE is published.
notes.explanation: Outside training, a twin is below VSSE only for seconds just after lift-off or just before landing.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 13 “Transition to Multiengine Airplanes”, “Spin Awareness”, PDF p. 18
notes.evidence: No engine failure should ever be introduced below safe, intentional one-engine inoperative speed (VSSE). If no VSSE is published, use VYSE. Other than training situations, the multiengine airplane is only operated below VSSE for mere seconds just after lift-off or during the last few dozen feet of altitude in preparation for landing.
uses: best single-engine rate of climb speed

notes.front: How much drag can a propeller windmilling at high rpm in the low blade-angle range produce?
notes.back: Parasite drag as great as that of the entire airframe.
notes.explanation: At these small blade angles the drag can make the aeroplane difficult or impossible to control.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 13 “Transition to Multiengine Airplanes”, “Feathering Propellers”, PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: At these small blade angles, the propeller windmilling at high revolutions per minute (rpm) can create enough drag to make the airplane difficult or impossible to control. A propeller windmilling at high speed in the low range of blade angles can produce parasite drag as great as the parasite drag of the entire airframe.

notes.front: Operating an aircraft on the water, what is your general duty towards vessels?
notes.back: Keep clear of all vessels as far as possible, avoid impeding their navigation, and give way to any craft given the right-of-way.
notes.explanation: The duty applies 'insofar as possible', and the other rules of the section set who has the right-of-way.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.115 Right-of-way rules: Water operations (eCFR), paragraph (a)
notes.evidence: Each person operating an aircraft on the water shall, insofar as possible, keep clear of all vessels and avoid impeding their navigation, and shall give way to any vessel or other aircraft that is given the right-of-way by any rule of this section.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: On the water, an aircraft and a vessel are on crossing courses. Which has the right-of-way?
notes.back: The one to the other's right.
notes.explanation: The same rule applies between two aircraft on the water.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.115 Right-of-way rules: Water operations (eCFR), paragraph (b)
notes.evidence: (b) Crossing. When aircraft, or an aircraft and a vessel, are on crossing courses, the aircraft or vessel to the other's right has the right-of-way.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: On the water, which craft has the right-of-way when one overtakes another?
notes.back: The one being overtaken; the overtaking craft must alter course to keep well clear.
notes.explanation: This applies to aircraft and vessels alike.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.115 Right-of-way rules: Water operations (eCFR), paragraph (d)
notes.evidence: (d) Overtaking. Each aircraft or vessel that is being overtaken has the right-of-way, and the one overtaking shall alter course to keep well clear.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: The seaplane task in the Airman Certification Standards expects you to know the causes of which two water-handling problems, and how to prevent or correct them?
notes.back: Porpoising and skipping.
notes.explanation: The same task also covers float and hull construction and its effect on seaplane performance.
notes.source: Private Pilot for Airplane Category ACS (FAA-S-ACS-6C), Area I, Task I, Water and Seaplane Characteristics, PDF p. 17
notes.evidence: PA.I.I.K2 Float and hull construction, and its effect on seaplane performance. PA.I.I.K3 Causes of porpoising and skipping, and the pilot action needed to prevent or correct these occurrences.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Besides marine navigation aids, which two kinds of zone must a seaplane applicant understand under the Airman Certification Standards?
notes.back: Naval vessel protection zones and no wake zones.
notes.explanation: Marine navigation aids themselves include buoys, beacons, lights, sound signals and range markers.
notes.source: Private Pilot for Airplane Category ACS (FAA-S-ACS-6C), Area I, Task I, Water and Seaplane Characteristics, PDF p. 17
notes.evidence: PA.I.I.K7 Marine navigation aids, such as buoys, beacons, lights, sound signals, and range markers. PA.I.I.K8 Naval vessel protection zones. PA.I.I.K9 No wake zones.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What are two features the Airman Certification Standards list as affecting the characteristics of a water surface?
notes.back: Any two, among others: surface wind, water current, floating debris.
notes.explanation: The list opens with the size and location of the water and whether areas are protected.
notes.source: Private Pilot for Airplane Category ACS (FAA-S-ACS-6C), Area I, Task I, Water and Seaplane Characteristics, PDF p. 17
notes.evidence: PA.I.I.K1 The characteristics of a water surface as affected by features, such as: PA.I.I.K1a a. Size and location PA.I.I.K1b b. Protected and unprotected areas PA.I.I.K1c c. Surface wind PA.I.I.K1d d. Direction and strength of water current PA.I.I.K1e e. Floating and partially submerged debris
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What are two of the seaplane after-landing procedures from which the evaluator must select at least one?
notes.back: Any two of: anchoring, docking and mooring, ramping/beaching.
notes.explanation: The evaluator chooses at least one of the three for the practical test.
notes.source: Private Pilot for Airplane Category ACS (FAA-S-ACS-6C), Area XII, Task B, Seaplane Post-Landing Procedures, PDF p. 72
notes.evidence: Note: The evaluator must select at least one after-landing procedure (anchoring, docking and mooring, or ramping/beaching).
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: After an engine failure in a twin, you need strong left rudder to keep straight, and your right foot is idle. Which engine has failed?
notes.back: B) The right engine
notes.explanation: Rudder pressure goes on the side of the operating engine, so the idle ('dead') foot is on the side of the dead engine.
notes.choices:
A) The left engine
B) The right engine
C) It cannot be told without the engine gauges
notes.choicesExplained: A: the left foot is working, so the left engine is the operating one. C: identification should rest mainly on the control inputs, not the gauges.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 13 “Transition to Multiengine Airplanes”, “Climb”, PDF p. 33
notes.evidence: In maintaining directional control, however, rudder pressure is exerted on the side (left or right) of the airplane with the operating engine. Thus, the “dead foot” is on the same side as the “dead engine.”

notes.front: Before a twin takeoff you chose a decision point. Just airborne, still short of that point, an engine fails. What does the handbook recommend?
notes.back: A) Reject the takeoff and land on whatever runway or surface lies ahead
notes.explanation: A decision point picked in advance settles the choice: before it, reject even if airborne.
notes.choices:
A) Reject the takeoff and land on whatever runway or surface lies ahead
B) Continue the climb on the good engine
C) Turn back to the runway at once
notes.choicesExplained: B: continuing is for failures after the decision point, and only if the performance exists. C: the handbook says to land on what lies essentially ahead.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 13 “Transition to Multiengine Airplanes”, “Performance and Limitations”, PDF p. 12
notes.evidence: The prudent multiengine pilot should pick a decision point in the takeoff and climb sequence in advance. If an engine fails before this point, the takeoff should be rejected, even if airborne, for a landing on whatever runway or surface lies essentially ahead.

notes.front: Taxiing a seaplane, you meet a boat approaching head-on. What must each of you do?
notes.back: B) Each alters course to the right to keep well clear
notes.explanation: The rule applies whenever aircraft, or an aircraft and a vessel, approach head-on or nearly so.
notes.choices:
A) The boat gives way because you are an aircraft
B) Each alters course to the right to keep well clear
C) Each alters course to the left
notes.choicesExplained: A: on the water, an aircraft must keep clear of vessels as far as possible. C: the rule is to the right.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.115 Right-of-way rules: Water operations (eCFR), paragraph (c)
notes.evidence: (c) Approaching head-on. When aircraft, or an aircraft and a vessel, are approaching head-on, or nearly so, each shall alter its course to the right to keep well clear.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: On a twin's airspeed indicator, what do the red radial line and the blue radial line stand for?
notes.back: Red: VMC, the loss of directional control. Blue: VYSE, the best performance with an engine inoperative.
notes.explanation: The handbook sums up the chapter as these two considerations: control and best performance after an engine failure.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 13 “Transition to Multiengine Airplanes”, “Chapter Summary”, PDF p. 37
notes.evidence: Much of this chapter discussed loss of directional control. How to obtain the best performance with an inoperative engine was also described in detail. These two considerations correspond to the red radial line (VMC) and the blue radial line (VYSE) on the airspeed indicator.
uses: minimum control speed with the critical engine inoperative
best single-engine rate of climb speed

notes.front: How do accelerate-stop distance and accelerate-go distance differ?
notes.back: Accelerate-stop: accelerate to rotation or lift-off speed, lose an engine, stop. Accelerate-go: after that failure, continue and climb to 50 feet.
notes.explanation: Accelerate-stop is measured as a runway length; accelerate-go as a horizontal distance to 50 feet.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 13 “Transition to Multiengine Airplanes”, “Performance and Limitations”, PDF p. 10
notes.evidence: runway length required to accelerate to a specified speed (either VR or VLOF, as specified by the manufacturer), experience an engine failure, and bring the airplane to a complete stop. [Figure 13-5A] ⦁ Accelerate-go distance is the horizontal distance required to continue the takeoff and climb to 50 feet
